books.section: Topic 4.8 Jackson and Federal Power, B. Contention Between Whites and American Indians over Western Lands
The Jackson Presidency and Jacksonian Democracy

stimulus.text: The portrait, published in 1838, shows Sequoyah (Se-Quo-Yah), a Cherokee leader, holding a tablet covered with the characters of the Cherokee syllabary, the writing system he invented. The Cherokee used the syllabary to print their own newspaper, the Cherokee Phoenix, beginning in 1828.
stimulus.source_note: Portrait 'Se-Quo-Yah,' McKenney-Hall series, drawn, printed and coloured at I. T. Bowen's Lithographic Establishment, Philadelphia, published 1838 (Library of Congress). Public domain; image viewed before writing.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The portrait and the Cherokee Phoenix best support which conclusion about the Cherokee in the 1820s and 1830s?

options.text: The Cherokee refused all contact with American settlers
options.misconception: Removal stories stress conflict, so it is easy to picture the Cherokee cut off from American life.

options.text: The Cherokee had no written language of their own before removal
options.misconception: A portrait of a Native leader invites the old assumption that his people had no writing of their own.

options.text: The Cherokee welcomed removal as protection
options.misconception: Jackson said removal would protect the tribes, so it is easy to think the Cherokee agreed.

options.text: The Cherokee had built their own written language and press

rationales.A: A Cherokee newspaper and a written language show deep engagement with American life, not refusal of all contact.
rationales.B: The tablet in the portrait is covered with Cherokee characters; Sequoyah's syllabary gave the Cherokee a written language.
rationales.C: The Cherokee fought removal in the courts and through their principal chief, John Ross; they did not welcome it.
rationales.D: Sequoyah holds his syllabary, and the Phoenix printed in it shows a Cherokee press at work a decade before removal.
rationales.general:
1. Read the tablet. Sequoyah holds a page of Cherokee characters, the syllabary he invented.
2. Read the newspaper's date. The Cherokee Phoenix began printing in 1828, ten years before the forced march west.
3. Put the two together. A people with its own writing and press had built American-style institutions before removal came.
Remember: a portrait's prop can be the whole argument — ask what the sitter chose to hold.

figures.caption: Se-Quo-Yah, 1838. Sequoyah holds a tablet of Cherokee syllabary characters.
figures.alt: A portrait of Sequoyah, a Cherokee leader in a red turban, holding a tablet covered with the characters of the Cherokee syllabary
